name: Crosslight Festival
description: Held over the five nights surrounding the winter solstice, Crosslight began in 2195 as a spontaneous overlap of three simultaneous traditions: a Shelf ward's communal fire-lighting ritual derived from mixed West African and Scandinavian heritage practices, a Tier 3 neighborhood's projection-art open night, and a corponation-sponsored 'Winter Luminance' product showcase — all of which fell on the same December weekend by accident. The collision produced something none of the three intended: a city-wide tradition of public light-making in which every tier participates through radically different means, unified only by the act of adding light to the longest darkness of the year.
cultural_impact: Crosslight is the closest thing GLMZ has to a genuinely shared holiday — not because it was designed that way, but because it accidentally accommodates every budget and every aesthetic simultaneously. It is also the one time of year when Shelf art is most visible to upper tiers, as the raw fire-and-found-object installations of Tier 1 communities are widely photographed and shared across the city's media networks, sometimes earning Shelf artists their only mainstream exposure.
key_figures: Ife Magnusson-Diallo (Shelf Ward 3 fire-artist whose 2195 bonfire installation is considered the founding act of Crosslight)
Projection collective VANTA BLOOM (Tier 3 artists whose annual solstice installation at the Confluence has become a Crosslight landmark)
Corsa Mehta-Lindqvist (the same Axiom-Helios PR architect who designed Dividend Day — her co-optation attempt in 2198 failed, making Crosslight her only acknowledged professional defeat)
locations: The Burn Grounds, Shelf Ward 3 (site of the original fire ritual, still the emotional heart of Crosslight)
Confluence Plaza, Tier 3 (VANTA BLOOM's annual projection site, open to all)
The Spire Canopy, Tier 5 (where bioluminescent geneware fashion shows double as the elite version of the light tradition)
story_hooks: Axiom-Helios has quietly purchased the air rights above the Burn Grounds and is planning to install a commercial projection system that will overlay the Shelf fires with branded imagery — and the announcement is timed to drop on the first night of Crosslight.

A Shelf fire-artist has created an installation this year using salvaged synthetic components that, when burned, produce an unexpected signal detectable on BCI frequencies — drawing attention from parties she never intended to reach.

A Tier 5 geneware designer whose Spire Canopy show has become a Crosslight institution wants to move the show to the Burn Grounds for one year as an artistic statement — and the Shelf community is deeply, vocally divided about whether to allow it.
origin_event: The accidental 2195 convergence of a Shelf communal fire ritual, a Tier 3 projection art open night, and a corponation Winter Luminance showcase on the same December weekend, which produced an unplanned cross-tier celebration that no single group could claim ownership of.
tier_observations: Tier 1 Shelf communities build large communal fires from salvaged materials, create found-object light sculptures, and observe the oldest version of the tradition with collective meals and open wards — the most communal and physically warm expression of the festival. Tier 2 and 3 residents string lights, attend public projection installations, and participate in neighborhood light-walks; some make the trip to the Burn Grounds, which has become a point of quiet pride. Tier 4 corporate households observe with expensive bioluminescent home decorations, curated light-art purchases, and private rooftop parties. Tier 5 Spire residents treat Crosslight as a fashion and geneware showcase season, with bioluminescent body modifications, light-reactive couture, and invitation-only sky events — the most expensive and most disconnected expression of a tradition that began in a Shelf ward with a match and a pile of salvage.
